usage: very common way to say you are unwell
common goodbye when someone is sick or it's cold
examples: My body is so tired today.
몸 + 피곤하다 to talk about being worn out
I'm sick, so I'm going to the hospital.
common reason to go to a clinic
If you exercise, your body gets healthy.
nuance: 몸 means the physical body as a whole, and 'my body hurts' (몸이 아파요) is the most natural everyday way to say you feel sick. It also appears in set phrases like 몸조심하세요 (take care) and 몸이 안 좋아요 (I don't feel well). Beginners use 몸 far more than the formal word 신체.
mistakes: Saying 나는 아파요 alone is fine, but to stress feeling unwell people say 몸이 아파요 — don't drop 몸이 when describing general sickness.
Don't confuse 몸 (body) with 봄 (spring); they look and sound similar but are different words.

usage: the soft part of the body
examples: I've gained a little weight lately.
I gain weight easily in winter.
nuance: 살 is the soft flesh of the body, and in daily life it is used constantly to talk about weight: 살이 찌다 (gain weight) and 살이 빠지다 / 살을 빼다 (lose weight). It can also mean the skin you can pinch, separate from 피부 which is the skin's surface. For weight, Koreans almost always say 살, not 체중.
mistakes: Use 살이 쪘어요 for 'gained weight,' not 살이 컸어요 — 크다 (to grow big) is wrong here.
Don't mix up 살 (flesh/age counter) with 쌀 (uncooked rice); the tense ㅆ sound changes the meaning.

examples: 피가 나다 = to bleed, the most common phrase
I fell and my knee bled.
I get scared when I see blood.
nuance: 피 is the plain, everyday word for blood, used whenever you cut yourself or bleed: 피가 나요 (I'm bleeding) is the phrase you'll hear and need most. The formal/medical word 혈액 appears on hospital forms (혈액형 = blood type), but in conversation you say 피. 코피 (nosebleed) is a handy compound to learn alongside it.
mistakes: For bleeding, say 피가 나요, not 피가 와요 — the verb is 나다 (to come out), not 오다.
Don't use the medical word 혈액 in casual speech about a cut; 피 is the natural choice.

examples: My lips get dry in winter.
I put lipstick on my lips.
입술 with a borrowed word 립스틱
My lips are blue because it's cold.
nuance: 입술 means the lips, and it is built from 입 (mouth) — but 입술 is specifically the lips, while 입 is the whole mouth/opening. It comes up a lot in winter (입술이 마르다 / 트다, chapped lips) and for cosmetics. Keep 입 and 입술 separate: you eat with your 입, you apply balm to your 입술.
mistakes: Don't say 입 when you mean the lips specifically — 입 is the mouth, 입술 is the lips.
Lips are usually treated as a pair, so you normally just say 입술, not 입술들.

examples: I burned my tongue on the hot soup.
I bit my tongue while eating.
nuance: 혀 is the tongue, the organ you taste and speak with. The most common beginner sentences are 혀를 데었어요 (I burned my tongue) and 혀를 깨물었어요 (I bit my tongue). It's a short, single-syllable word, so be careful to pronounce the 여 vowel clearly.
mistakes: Don't confuse 혀 (tongue) with 혜 or 햐; the vowel is 여, pronounced like 'hyuh.'
혀 is the body part; the sense 'taste' is 맛, so 'I taste it' is 맛을 봐요, not 혀를 봐요.

examples: My nails were long, so I clipped them.
nuance: 손톱 is a fingernail, formed from 손 (hand) plus 톱. Learn it together with its sibling 발톱 (toenail). The natural verb for trimming nails is 깎다 (to clip/shave), the same verb used for an apple peel or a haircut.
mistakes: To trim nails, use 손톱을 깎다, not 손톱을 자르다 — 깎다 is the idiomatic verb.
Don't mix up 손톱 (fingernail) and 발톱 (toenail); 손 is hand and 발 is foot.

examples: Your eyebrows are dark and pretty.
I drew my eyebrows looking in the mirror.
I have a mole above my eyebrow.
nuance: 눈썹 is the eyebrow, made from 눈 (eye) plus 썹. The closely related word 속눈썹 means eyelashes (속 = inside). Eyebrows come up often in describing faces and in makeup talk (눈썹을 그리다, to draw on brows).
mistakes: Don't confuse 눈썹 (eyebrow) with 속눈썹 (eyelash); 속 means 'inner.'
눈썹 is the brow, while 눈 alone is the eye — keep them distinct.

examples: 키가 작다 with a softening pattern
My younger sibling has grown a lot taller.
키가 크다 in past tense = grew
nuance: 키 means a person's height, and you describe it with 크다/작다: 키가 커요 (tall), 키가 작아요 (short). Note the verb is 크다 (big), not 길다 (long) — Korean treats height as 'big/small,' not 'long.' In the past tense 키가 컸어요 also means 'grew taller.'
mistakes: For tall, say 키가 커요, not 키가 길어요 — height uses 크다, not 길다.
Don't confuse this 키 (height) with the borrowed 키 meaning 'key'; context tells them apart.

examples: The singer has a really nice voice.
I have a cold, so I've lost my voice.
Your voice sounds quiet on the phone.
nuance: 목소리 is the voice, literally 목 (throat) plus 소리 (sound). It is used both for compliments (목소리가 좋아요) and for health (감기 때문에 목소리가 안 나와요, losing your voice from a cold). Don't reduce it to just 소리, which means any sound, not specifically a person's voice.
mistakes: For a person's voice use 목소리, not just 소리 — 소리 is any sound.
'Loud voice' is 목소리가 커요 (big), not 목소리가 높아요 (high), which describes pitch instead.

usage: idiom: 'laugh till your navel falls out'
examples: The top is short, so my belly button shows.
The baby's belly button is really small.
It was so funny I almost split my sides.
nuance: 배꼽 is the belly button, sitting on the 배 (stomach). It's an easy, concrete body word and also appears in the fun idiom 배꼽 빠지게 웃다 (to laugh so hard your navel falls out). Pair it with 배 (belly/stomach) when learning the torso.
mistakes: Don't confuse 배꼽 (navel) with 배 (belly/stomach as a whole); the 배꼽 is just the small navel point.
Remember the tense ㄲ in 배꼽 — writing 배곱 is a spelling error.

examples: I got angry and clenched my fist tight.
The apple is about the size of a fist.
I had rice balls for lunch.
nuance: 주먹 is a clenched fist, and the natural verb is 쥐다 (to grip) — 주먹을 쥐다. It doubles as a handy size reference (주먹만 해요, about fist-sized) and lives inside the food word 주먹밥 (hand-pressed rice ball). It's a concrete, useful word even for beginners.
mistakes: To make a fist, say 주먹을 쥐다, not 주먹을 잡다 — 쥐다 (grip) fits, 잡다 (grab) does not here.
Don't confuse 주먹 (fist) with 손 (the open hand); a 주먹 is specifically the closed hand.

usage: the back of my hand is dry
to apply on the back of the hand
examples: The backs of my hands are dry in winter.
I put hand cream on the back of my hand.
I wiped the sweat with the back of my hand.
nuance: 손등 is the back of the hand, built from 손 (hand) plus 등 (back). Its opposite is 손바닥 (palm). The 등 part is the same word used for the back of the body, so 손등 literally means 'hand-back.' It's useful for skincare and everyday gestures.
mistakes: Don't confuse 손등 (back of hand) with 손바닥 (palm); they are opposite sides.
손등 is one word, so don't insert a space — write 손등, not 손 등.

examples: I caught a cold and my throat hurts.
My throat was sore, so I drank water.
A fish bone got stuck in my throat.
nuance: 목구멍 is the inner throat passage, literally 목 (neck/throat) plus 구멍 (hole). In casual speech people often just say 목이 아파요 for a sore throat, but 목구멍 specifies the inside passage, useful at the doctor. Learn both 목 and 목구멍 together.
mistakes: 목 can mean both neck and throat; use 목구멍 when you specifically mean the inner throat.
Don't drop the ㅁ — it's 목구멍, not 목구머.

usage: casual way to say mentally worn out
examples: I studied a lot, so my brain is tired.
The human brain is really amazing.
When you sleep, your brain rests.
nuance: 뇌 is the brain as a physical organ. In everyday conversation about thinking or memory, Koreans more often say 머리 (head/mind) — for example 머리가 좋다 (to be smart). Use 뇌 for the actual organ (health, science), and 머리 for casual talk about thinking.
mistakes: For 'smart,' say 머리가 좋다, not 뇌가 좋다 — casual mental ability uses 머리.
뇌 is one syllable pronounced 'nwe'; don't split it into two beats.
